Wildlife Snares

By: Annalise Lubbe | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Illegal snares are on the increase in the Cape Peninsula and Boland as small animals are being killed for their meat and body parts. Carte Blanche investigates.

Unique Selling Point:
Illegal Wildlife Snares are killing our wildlife.. Since Covid-19 there has been a dramatic increase in the number of snares being set by poachers in the city’s green belt areas and Table Mountain National Park. Animals like franklin, porcupine, duikers, caracal and mongoose living in the urban edge of the park are being trapped indiscriminately - and we are not talking syndicate level here. Traps are being set by one or two people and snares are usually set close to residential areas like Fishoek and Noordhoek Wetlands. Greenbelts like Constantia and Klaaschenbosh are also targeted.


Summary:
Globally there is a major threat for wildlife living on the urban edge of towns, cities and farmland as their habitat becomes fragmented and their natural prey disappear. The Western Cape is no different. From the Cape Peninsula to the Boland, small animals like mongoose, porcupine, caracal, duikertjie and baboons are forced into densely populated areas where they become easy target for poachers: meat for the pot; skin, bones and organs for the muti trade; and souvenirs for tourist, fuelling the trade. Added to this list is the Cape Leopard. Once the apex predator on the peninsula this majestic animal fled into the mountainous area of the Boland and crossed onto farms where they too have become a target for poachers.

Crude snares are made from electric wire, nylon rope and fishing lines are shaped into a noose to catch the animal around the foot, body or neck. Once caught in the snare, the noose tightens and the trapped animal faces a cruel slow death. Snares aren’t checked regularly and so most animals are only found days later.

In the Cape Peninsula snares are found mainly in the greenbelt areas and on the fringes of the Table Mountain National Park. With limited SANParks rangers, honorary rangers have been called upon to assist with the patrolling and removal of snares. Organisations like the Cape Leopard Trust and the Urban Caracal Project have provided vital scientific data and support on the ground in the quest of protecting the wildlife and ensuring their sustainable future. The forestry areas in Klaasenbosch and Alphen trails in Constantia have recently come under the spotlight when a concerned citizen found dozens of snares in a thick part of the forest where alien trees have been removed.


Further information:
PHD graduate Gabriella Leigton, who has been doing research on caracals for the Urban Caracal Project on ‘living on the edge of urbanisation’, works closely with Table Mountain National park and honorary rangers to eradicate snares. She said a juvenile female caracal had recently been found with a snare on its paw near Eagles Nest wine estate above Constantia Main Road. “We’re not sure where she picked up the snare but likely in the Constantia area as her movement was very limited by the injury, and she had not been able to hunt for weeks. She died of her wounds.

Eyes and ears are important as Jeffrey Heath, a resident of Wynberg, found who has been clearing snares from the Klaasenbosch greenbelt whilst clearing aliens. He counted dozens of wire snares from the area since the start of the pandemic. He contacted honorary ranger, Robert Stella who are on a constant patrol and working closely with people who report snares. “The poachers do not discriminate and snare guinea fowl, mongoose, grysbokkies, duiker, caracal, baboon, tortoise, genet and domestic cats and dogs,” said Stella. “A Constantia baboon died from a snare around its neck. We’ve also found bones of dead animals with the snare still around their necks.”

Jon Friedman, manager of the wildlife unit of the Cape of Good Hope SPCA responds to regular calls to retrieve animals stuck in snares. “Snares offer a cruel, agonising and drawn-out death to any animal that gets caught in one”, he says. He is also an honorary ranger and does regular patrols of the Fish Hoek area below the caves and Noordhoek wetland areas. He says snaring also occurs on the wine farm fences where workers try to scare off baboons from raiding the crop. He is often called out to assist a baboon with a snare still attached which the SPCA then has to remove. In some instances the baboon has suffered only minor injuries and can be released again to join its troup.

Anita Wilkinson, biologist and researcher at the Cape Leopard Trust, says they have launched an anti-snare project in 2019 in the Boland district in an effort to clamp down on the illegal snaring happening across farmlands, conservancies and on the urban fringes of towns. In an extensive field study and interviews farm labourers admitted to regular involvement in snaring activity. Small antelope, porcupine and guinea-fowl were the species most frequently caught in wire snares. This is significant as it is the main prey species of the leopard that are threatened by livestock farming, urbansiation and limited food source. In the study they covered 770km on foot and recovered 449 snare traps on 118 properties surrounding the mountain wilderness in the Boland.

Zwelethongo is a traditional healer from the Transkei living in Kyamandi in Stellenbosch who believes in the healing power of the plant and animal products for healing and will share her ideas with us. Booker, a poacher also living in Kyamandi in Stellenbosch, grew up in the Transkei hunting for wild animals as part of their meat intake and have continued catching wild animals here in the Boland using snares to catch small duikers and porcupine for their meat.

The story: We will track some of the footpaths used by the poachers where snares are typically found. We will see the close proximity of the houses to the greenbelt and the easy access it provides where no fences deter poachers. We will also go into the forestry area of the greenbelt in Constantia to get a feel for this piece of paradise frequented by joggers, dog-walkers and people on horseback and the well hidden areas where the snares were found by Jeaffrey when clearing the alien plants. Links will be in these areas. We have access to all the photos and some video clips of the people we interview which will give visual evidence of the material used, the locations, the method, the environment and the animals in the traps. We will interview a poacher from a township in Stellenbosch who will share his snaring practices with us and speak openly about his preference for bushmeat and how he catches his prey. A traditional healer from Kyamandi in Stellenbosch will tell us about the animal products she uses from wild animals like porcupine, caracal skins and her belief in its healing properties. The poacher showed us a video clip of a small envelope being caught and a few images of the bush meat to use in the story. Both the traditional healer and the poacher asked not to be named and their identity to be hidden.

Script:


Final Script: Wildlife snaring
Date: 27 September 2022
Duration: 10 minutes
Up sound

V/O It is 8am and we’re meeting two rangers out on patrol: Jon Friedman from the Cape of Good Hope SPCA; and Robert Stella, an honorary ranger from SANParks Table Mountain National Park.

Up sound

V/O This morning, within a stone’s throw of suburbia, they’re scouting the greenbelt near Fish Hoek in Cape Town on the lookout for snares set by poachers.

Link: I am about to join Jon and Robert on a path where there is a likelihood of a snare hidden under a tree or a thick bush. Let’s see what we go find.

V/O A snare is a rudimentary piece of wire, shaped into a loop, anchored down in an area known for animals.

Robert Stella: So here is a perfect example of where a poacher will set a snare, it is a main track, animals go in and out here on a daily basis.

V/O Robert and Jon are trained trackers: Footprints in the sand, discarded material and broken vegetation are possible clues helping to hunt down suspected poachers.

Up sound

Jon Friedman: Wildlife Supervisor - Cape of Good Hope SPCA: We will be able to go through the material left behind, we might find a clue here, a knife or something that might be used in snaring material.

V/O Even though we are close to busy suburban Cape Town, the range of animals found here may surprise you.

Robert Stella: Honorary ranger: SANParks So it is anything from a mongoose, guinea fowl, grys bokkie, caracal unfortunately.

V/O So no shortage of animals. But why the need to trap them?

Robert Stella: The poachers they target anything, and we feel the main reason, obviously there is muti and supply the meat trade. The skins are sold on the market like genet skins, caracal skins, mongoose skins.

Jon Friedman: This phenomenon of snaring really became an issue around the covid-19 lockdown. As things get tougher maybe for certain segments of society things like snaring become more attractive so being able to come out into an area like this, harvest some wildlife and get some money from that.

Link: So we haven’t found any traces of snares this morning but this is definitely one of the hot spots targeted by poachers.

V/O The Noordhoek wetlands - not far from Fish Hoek valley - are another hotspot. Sandwiched between a luxury housing estate, and Masiphumelele, a fast growing township of about 30 000 people, the wetlands are a convenient hunting ground.

UP sound

V/O Gabriella Leighton of the Urban Caracal Project has conducted an in-depth study of the effect of urbanisation on wildlife, focusing on the caracal, a species of wild cat.

Gabriella Leighton: Post-Doctoral Researcher - Urban Caracal Project: So the major threat to caracals on the Cape Peninsula is being hit by cars. And the second major thing is exposure to disease and pesticide which is a uniquely urban threat they face but one of the third most important threats we detected is poaching and particularly snaring, and we have detected at least 12 individuals that have been caught over the last 4,5 years in snares or some kind of trap on the Peninsula.

Claire Mawisa: So what happens once we found a caracal caught in a snare?

Gabriella Leighton: Generally what happens when an animals is caught in a snare, what happens is a wire loop that tightens around the animal, usually it is the leg or the abdomen and it is a really horrible way to die because essentially the wire just constrict and constrict until that animal passes away from organ failure or the injuries or some kind of infection.

V/O Our next stop is the greenbelt in Constantia, just a few kilometers away.

LINK: Even here poachers lay deadly snares for small wild animals.

V/O Jeffrey Heath, a frequent visitor to these forests, spotted a wire noose in the undergrowth whilst clearing alien plants.

Jeffrey Heath: I discovered that the poacher was cutting down some of the small cotton Easter trees to make fences and walls for the animal to go towards the snare. The snares were made out of wire with a noose at the end. Every time I was coming back here I would find more and then more and then another.

V/O Snaring is illegal causing animals unimaginable suffering but that’s often the case with legal hunting, too. So is this a case of the law being at odds with tradition, unfairly targeting the poor? Is it possible to find solutions where people’s livelihoods - and even identity - are at stake? Or is this a space where custom and conservation will forever collide?

Fade to black…Pause

Poacher: When I was a young boy I was shooting the birds. I learned it from my elder brothers. But hunting, as I see it, I hate the word poaching.

V/O This long-time hunter from the Eastern Cape has asked us to hide his identity. There’s no difference, he says, between shooting an animal and snaring it.

Poacher: I have my work. That means I can afford to buy food, but I continue with hunting.

V/O He lives in an informal settlement in the Cape’s Boland close to a greenbelt. He has a taste for a range of wild animals.

Poacher: I like bushmeat. I like the bushmeat. I normally catch the steenboks. Some kind of buck and the porcupine. There at home I normally catch the caracal.

V/O It sounds matter of fact…..until he produces a video of a small antelope he recently caught in a snare.

Up sound: Cellphone video clip sound: Ikukrwelile? (Did it scratch you?) Iza kuqhawula. (It’s going to escape.)

V/O The meat is for the pot, the skin and other parts will be sold.

Poacher: I also selling parts to the sangoma like the skin. The last buck I catched it was in June. That skin was R450.

Up sound of song

V/O Traditional medicines are widely used here in Africa with up to 80% of the continent turning to natural remedies, according to the World Health Organisation. Plants, herbs and animal parts are key ingredients.
Pause
V/O A traditional healer invites us into her sacred space where we ask her about the caracal.

Traditional healer: Ndiyayisebenzisa eyasendle ikati but enkulu. (I do use wild cats, but the big one.) (I haven’t had one recently though.)

V/O She also explains how she uses porcupine intestines to cure stomach cramps.

Traditional healer: Ndikhuphe olwa lusu. Ndiloneke, lome. (Once it dies, I open it up and take out the intestines and leave them out to dry.) Ukoma kwalo, ndilungqushe, libe fine. (When it is dry, I grind it fine.) Laba fine, ndiluthathe (Once it is ground, I take it) ndidibanise neminye imithi yam. (I mix it with my other herbs.)

V/O Our last stop is the Bottelary conservancy in the Boland where two small antelopes and a caracal were recently found trapped in snares. We’re met by Anita Wilkinson from The Cape Leopard Trust.

Up sound - So this is a typical animal path that might be used to put a snare.

V/O For a better understanding of the threats posed to leopard and other animals, Anita and her team want to know why and where snaring occurs most in the Boland. A field worker was sent out to gather research.

Anita Wilkinson: Senior Researcher - Cape Leopard Trust: He walked about 1400km by foot on these properties and he removed more than 600 snares from these properties, and from that study it was evident that a lot of farm workers also set snares and the animals they target are small game and it is usually for the pot.

V/O Globally, the main threats to predators such as leopards are habitat loss and fragmentation; the loss of prey animals; and direct persecution by humans.

Anita Wilkinson: So if there is indiscriminate hunting with the snares many of the prey species are taken away and the prey basis of the leopard decreases and that affects the survival chances of the leopard.

Claire Mawisa; What will happen if the snaring issue is not brought under control? If it just continues and escalates?

Anita Wilkinson: So in parts of west Africa there is the empty forest syndrome and I think that is what we would get, empty fynbos. There is just no animals left in the landscape.

V/O And if that’s the catastrophic result of the clash between conservation and tradition, then everyone loses. Workable solutions, though, appear in short supply.

Poacher: If I catch an animal and law enforcement comes, then I have to run. But to who does this animal belong to? Because this animal doesn’t belong to anyone.

Traditional healer: Khon’ akukho raythi but yimpilo yethu. (Look, it’s not right. But it’s our way of life.) Asinakwenza ngakumbi. (We can’t do it any other way.)

V/O There are fewer than 60 caracals left in the Cape Peninsula. Without bold action, their survival and that of numerous other species here and in the Boland is at risk.
_________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

SUNDAY PROMO
Claire Mawisa: Cape town, a city surrounded by natural beauty where we should be living in harmony side by side with our wildlife.

Gabriella Leighton: The Noordhoek wetlands is a major snaring hotspot. The sanparks honorary rangers often do snare patrol here and they picked up hundreds of snares over the years.

Claire Mawisa: Snares made from wire and nylon are set in the undergrowth catching animals and causing them to die a cruel and painful death.

__________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

Promo one: 21 seconds
V/O In the Cape Peninsula and Boland poachers have targeted small wild animals, killing them for the pot and for use in traditional medicines.
Jon Friedman: Back in April we had a case of a caracal who got snared through her backfoot using bicycle brake cable and it actually chewed through that cable.

Promo two: 21 seconds
V/O Wild animals living on the edge of the city’s green belt and the Table Mountain National Park are being killed indiscriminately by poachers, who set snares to catch their prey.
Gabriella Leighton: When an animal is caught in a snare it is a wire loop that tightens around the animal, usually it is the leg or the abdomen and it is a really horrible way to die.

Promo three: 11 seconds
V/O Snaring is rife on the Cape Peninsula and in the Boland area - the natural habitat of many small wild animals are targeted by poachers as a food source and for use in traditional medicines.

Robert Stella: Honorary ranger: SANParks So it is anything from a mongoose, guinea fowl, grys bokkie, caracal unfortunately. V/O So no shortage of animals. But why the need to trap them? Robert Stella: The poachers they target anything, and we feel the main reason, obviously there is muti and supply the meat trade. The skins are sold on the market like genet skins, caracal skins, mongoose skins. Jon Friedman: This phenomenon of snaring really became an issue around the covid-19 lockdown. As things get tougher maybe for certain segments of society things like snaring become more attractive so being able to come out into an area like this, harvest some wildlife and get some money from that. Link: So we haven’t found any traces of snares this morning but this is definitely one of the hot spots targeted by poachers. V/O The Noordhoek wetlands - not far from Fish Hoek valley - are another hotspot. Sandwiched between a luxury housing estate, and Masiphumelele, a fast growing township of about 30 000 people, the wetlands are a convenient hunting ground. UP sound V/O Gabriella Leighton of the Urban Caracal Project has conducted an in-depth study of the effect of urbanisation on wildlife, focusing on the caracal, a species of wild cat. Gabriella Leighton: Post-Doctoral Researcher - Urban Caracal Project: So the major threat to caracals on the Cape Peninsula is being hit by cars. And the second major thing is exposure to disease and pesticide which is a uniquely urban threat they face but one of the third most important threats we detected is poaching and particularly snaring, and we have detected at least 12 individuals that have been caught over the last 4,5 years in snares or some kind of trap on the Peninsula. Claire Mawisa: So what happens once we found a caracal caught in a snare? Gabriella Leighton: Generally what happens when an animals is caught in a snare, what happens is a wire loop that tightens around the animal, usually it is the leg or the abdomen and it is a really horrible way to die because essentially the wire just constrict and constrict until that animal passes away from organ failure or the injuries or some kind of infection. V/O Our next stop is the greenbelt in Constantia, just a few kilometers away. LINK: Even here poachers lay deadly snares for small wild animals. V/O Jeffrey Heath, a frequent visitor to these forests, spotted a wire noose in the undergrowth whilst clearing alien plants. Jeffrey Heath: I discovered that the poacher was cutting down some of the small cotton Easter trees to make fences and walls for the animal to go towards the snare. The snares were made out of wire with a noose at the end. Every time I was coming back here I would find more and then more and then another. V/O Snaring is illegal causing animals unimaginable suffering but that’s often the case with legal hunting, too. So is this a case of the law being at odds with tradition, unfairly targeting the poor? Is it possible to find solutions where people’s livelihoods - and even identity - are at stake? Or is this a space where custom and conservation will forever collide? Fade to black…Pause Poacher: When I was a young boy I was shooting the birds. I learned it from my elder brothers. But hunting, as I see it, I hate the word poaching. V/O This long-time hunter from the Eastern Cape has asked us to hide his identity. There’s no difference, he says, between shooting an animal and snaring it. Poacher: I have my work. That means I can afford to buy food, but I continue with hunting. V/O He lives in an informal settlement in the Cape’s Boland close to a greenbelt. He has a taste for a range of wild animals. Poacher: I like bushmeat. I like the bushmeat. I normally catch the steenboks. Some kind of buck and the porcupine. There at home I normally catch the caracal. V/O It sounds matter of fact…..until he produces a video of a small antelope he recently caught in a snare. Up sound: Cellphone video clip sound: Ikukrwelile? (Did it scratch you?) Iza kuqhawula. (It’s going to escape.) V/O The meat is for the pot, the skin and other parts will be sold. Poacher: I also selling parts to the sangoma like the skin. The last buck I catched it was in June. That skin was R450. Up sound of song V/O Traditional medicines are widely used here in Africa with up to 80% of the continent turning to natural remedies, according to the World Health Organisation. Plants, herbs and animal parts are key ingredients. Pause V/O A traditional healer invites us into her sacred space where we ask her about the caracal. Traditional healer: Ndiyayisebenzisa eyasendle ikati but enkulu. (I do use wild cats, but the big one.) (I haven’t had one recently though.) V/O She also explains how she uses porcupine intestines to cure stomach cramps. Traditional healer: Ndikhuphe olwa lusu. Ndiloneke, lome. (Once it dies, I open it up and take out the intestines and leave them out to dry.) Ukoma kwalo, ndilungqushe, libe fine. (When it is dry, I grind it fine.) Laba fine, ndiluthathe (Once it is ground, I take it) ndidibanise neminye imithi yam. (I mix it with my other herbs.) V/O Our last stop is the Bottelary conservancy in the Boland where two small antelopes and a caracal were recently found trapped in snares. We’re met by Anita Wilkinson from The Cape Leopard Trust. Up sound - So this is a typical animal path that might be used to put a snare. V/O For a better understanding of the threats posed to leopard and other animals, Anita and her team want to know why and where snaring occurs most in the Boland. A field worker was sent out to gather research. Anita Wilkinson: Senior Researcher - Cape Leopard Trust: He walked about 1400km by foot on these properties and he removed more than 600 snares from these properties, and from that study it was evident that a lot of farm workers also set snares and the animals they target are small game and it is usually for the pot. V/O Globally, the main threats to predators such as leopards are habitat loss and fragmentation; the loss of prey animals; and direct persecution by humans. Anita Wilkinson: So if there is indiscriminate hunting with the snares many of the prey species are taken away and the prey basis of the leopard decreases and that affects the survival chances of the leopard. Claire Mawisa; What will happen if the snaring issue is not brought under control? If it just continues and escalates? Anita Wilkinson: So in parts of west Africa there is the empty forest syndrome and I think that is what we would get, empty fynbos. There is just no animals left in the landscape. V/O And if that’s the catastrophic result of the clash between conservation and tradition, then everyone loses. Workable solutions, though, appear in short supply. Poacher: If I catch an animal and law enforcement comes, then I have to run. But to who does this animal belong to? Because this animal doesn’t belong to anyone. Traditional healer: Khon’ akukho raythi but yimpilo yethu. (Look, it’s not right. But it’s our way of life.) Asinakwenza ngakumbi. (We can’t do it any other way.) V/O There are fewer than 60 caracals left in the Cape Peninsula. Without bold action, their survival and that of numerous other species here and in the Boland is at risk. _________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ SUNDAY PROMO Claire Mawisa: Cape town, a city surrounded by natural beauty where we should be living in harmony side by side with our wildlife. Gabriella Leighton: The Noordhoek wetlands is a major snaring hotspot. The sanparks honorary rangers often do snare patrol here and they picked up hundreds of snares over the years. Claire Mawisa: Snares made from wire and nylon are set in the undergrowth catching animals and causing them to die a cruel and painful death. __________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promo one: 21 seconds V/O In the Cape Peninsula and Boland poachers have targeted small wild animals, killing them for the pot and for use in traditional medicines. Jon Friedman: Back in April we had a case of a caracal who got snared through her backfoot using bicycle brake cable and it actually chewed through that cable. Promo two: 21 seconds V/O Wild animals living on the edge of the city’s green belt and the Table Mountain National Park are being killed indiscriminately by poachers, who set snares to catch their prey. Gabriella Leighton: When an animal is caught in a snare it is a wire loop that tightens around the animal, usually it is the leg or the abdomen and it is a really horrible way to die. Promo three: 11 seconds V/O Snaring is rife on the Cape Peninsula and in the Boland area - the natural habitat of many small wild animals are targeted by poachers as a food source and for use in traditional medicines. ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Wildlife Snares (6218 ) Annalise Lubbe 27 September 2022

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Illegal snares are on the increase in the Cape Peninsula and Boland as small animals are being killed for their meat and body parts. Carte Blanche investigates.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Illegal Wildlife Snares are killing our wildlife.. Since Covid-19 there has been a dramatic increase in the number of snares being set by poachers in the city’s green belt areas and Table Mountain National Park. Animals like franklin, porcupine, duikers, caracal and mongoose living in the urban edge of the park are being trapped indiscriminately - and we are not talking syndicate level here. Traps are being set by one or two people and snares are usually set close to residential areas like Fishoek and Noordhoek Wetlands. Greenbelts like Constantia and Klaaschenbosh are also targeted.
metadata.Summary: Globally there is a major threat for wildlife living on the urban edge of towns, cities and farmland as their habitat becomes fragmented and their natural prey disappear. The Western Cape is no different. From the Cape Peninsula to the Boland, small animals like mongoose, porcupine, caracal, duikertjie and baboons are forced into densely populated areas where they become easy target for poachers: meat for the pot; skin, bones and organs for the muti trade; and souvenirs for tourist, fuelling the trade. Added to this list is the Cape Leopard. Once the apex predator on the peninsula this majestic animal fled into the mountainous area of the Boland and crossed onto farms where they too have become a target for poachers. Crude snares are made from electric wire, nylon rope and fishing lines are shaped into a noose to catch the animal around the foot, body or neck. Once caught in the snare, the noose tightens and the trapped animal faces a cruel slow death. Snares aren’t checked regularly and so most animals are only found days later. In the Cape Peninsula snares are found mainly in the greenbelt areas and on the fringes of the Table Mountain National Park. With limited SANParks rangers, honorary rangers have been called upon to assist with the patrolling and removal of snares. Organisations like the Cape Leopard Trust and the Urban Caracal Project have provided vital scientific data and support on the ground in the quest of protecting the wildlife and ensuring their sustainable future. The forestry areas in Klaasenbosch and Alphen trails in Constantia have recently come under the spotlight when a concerned citizen found dozens of snares in a thick part of the forest where alien trees have been removed.
metadata.Further information: PHD graduate Gabriella Leigton, who has been doing research on caracals for the Urban Caracal Project on ‘living on the edge of urbanisation’, works closely with Table Mountain National park and honorary rangers to eradicate snares. She said a juvenile female caracal had recently been found with a snare on its paw near Eagles Nest wine estate above Constantia Main Road. “We’re not sure where she picked up the snare but likely in the Constantia area as her movement was very limited by the injury, and she had not been able to hunt for weeks. She died of her wounds. Eyes and ears are important as Jeffrey Heath, a resident of Wynberg, found who has been clearing snares from the Klaasenbosch greenbelt whilst clearing aliens. He counted dozens of wire snares from the area since the start of the pandemic. He contacted honorary ranger, Robert Stella who are on a constant patrol and working closely with people who report snares. “The poachers do not discriminate and snare guinea fowl, mongoose, grysbokkies, duiker, caracal, baboon, tortoise, genet and domestic cats and dogs,” said Stella. “A Constantia baboon died from a snare around its neck. We’ve also found bones of dead animals with the snare still around their necks.” Jon Friedman, manager of the wildlife unit of the Cape of Good Hope SPCA responds to regular calls to retrieve animals stuck in snares. “Snares offer a cruel, agonising and drawn-out death to any animal that gets caught in one”, he says. He is also an honorary ranger and does regular patrols of the Fish Hoek area below the caves and Noordhoek wetland areas. He says snaring also occurs on the wine farm fences where workers try to scare off baboons from raiding the crop. He is often called out to assist a baboon with a snare still attached which the SPCA then has to remove. In some instances the baboon has suffered only minor injuries and can be released again to join its troup. Anita Wilkinson, biologist and researcher at the Cape Leopard Trust, says they have launched an anti-snare project in 2019 in the Boland district in an effort to clamp down on the illegal snaring happening across farmlands, conservancies and on the urban fringes of towns. In an extensive field study and interviews farm labourers admitted to regular involvement in snaring activity. Small antelope, porcupine and guinea-fowl were the species most frequently caught in wire snares. This is significant as it is the main prey species of the leopard that are threatened by livestock farming, urbansiation and limited food source. In the study they covered 770km on foot and recovered 449 snare traps on 118 properties surrounding the mountain wilderness in the Boland. Zwelethongo is a traditional healer from the Transkei living in Kyamandi in Stellenbosch who believes in the healing power of the plant and animal products for healing and will share her ideas with us. Booker, a poacher also living in Kyamandi in Stellenbosch, grew up in the Transkei hunting for wild animals as part of their meat intake and have continued catching wild animals here in the Boland using snares to catch small duikers and porcupine for their meat. The story: We will track some of the footpaths used by the poachers where snares are typically found. We will see the close proximity of the houses to the greenbelt and the easy access it provides where no fences deter poachers. We will also go into the forestry area of the greenbelt in Constantia to get a feel for this piece of paradise frequented by joggers, dog-walkers and people on horseback and the well hidden areas where the snares were found by Jeaffrey when clearing the alien plants. Links will be in these areas. We have access to all the photos and some video clips of the people we interview which will give visual evidence of the material used, the locations, the method, the environment and the animals in the traps. We will interview a poacher from a township in Stellenbosch who will share his snaring practices with us and speak openly about his preference for bushmeat and how he catches his prey. A traditional healer from Kyamandi in Stellenbosch will tell us about the animal products she uses from wild animals like porcupine, caracal skins and her belief in its healing properties. The poacher showed us a video clip of a small envelope being caught and a few images of the bush meat to use in the story. Both the traditional healer and the poacher asked not to be named and their identity to be hidden.
